doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Music education in Chicago high schools
summary: Levy remembers Chicago school bands with loaned instruments, private lessons and mandatory music appreciation, which are gone today.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yeah, that’s interesting. You know I guess you can go to college now and you can take the business of music, you know?

Yeah, that’s a good thing. Because they no longer do, like when Milt and I came along, in high school, there was like it is in college now. I mean they had these bands and every high school had a band in Chicago and I remember the professor who taught music in Phillips High School where Milt went. It was just perfect. You’d walk in and you’d get private lessons from him plus rehearsing, you know playing with the band and everything, and it developed some great musicians. And a lot of them would walk in and didn’t even have instruments to play. You’d come along and the kid, what they would do, they’d ask you, “what do you want to play?” And if there was an instrument left that you wanted to play, most of the time the trumpets and the saxophones would go first, and there’d only be so many of those. And nobody wanted the violins or that kind of stuff. Most of them wanted the horns, and guitar was, forget about that there was no such thing. I remember John Collins, the banjo [guitar] player, started out playing banjo. But anyway, they had instruments for the kids. And they had a certain number of instruments and you’d use it the whole time that you were in the school, the four years that you were there you’d have this instrument to play and learn on and everything, and practice, and take it home and all that. But all that’s gone. You don’t reach that now until you get to the college stage. There are some high school bands around the country, but not too many.

Well a lot of the people we’ve talked to have talked about their great high school experience and it’s amazing the congregation of people that were in Chicago for instance, the famous names that all came out of there in that time period.

It was great. And that was the period when most of them came out. Because they had that music education. It was a part of the training that you got. You had to have that. Everybody had to have a certain amount of music. Everybody, in all the classes, no matter what your majors were, you had to have a music class. They called it music appreciation, where they’d play records of the, you know, the classical records, and you had to identify who wrote this, whether it was Bach or Beethoven or whoever, you know, was the composer. And you got to learn a lot about the general culture of music. And it was a great experience in those days. And it’s unfortunate that these youngsters now, who need it, to me, more than ever, they really need this. They don’t get it.
